how_it_wins:
The table sees Edgar Markov and shields up for combat. Let them. This deck kills with triggers, and the ignition never has to be drawn: every Vampire spell you cast mints a token straight from the command zone. No setup card to protect, no key turn to telegraph. You cast cheap Vampires — eleven of them cost two or less — and the machine runs itself.

The kill is conversion. Five cards turn every arriving body into table-wide damage: Purphoros, God of the Forge, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Corpse Knight and Witty Roastmaster. Stack 009 is the whole plan in one exchange — one two-mana Vampire, three payoffs and a doubler on board, twelve damage to every opponent, table dead. You draw a converter by turn 6 in 62.6% of games. So your early turns have one job: land a converter and a multiplier, then keep casting Vampires into them.

The wipe is coming — plan to get paid for it. Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant drain as your board dies, and eminence rebuilds from a zone no sweeper touches. So commit in waves: deploy the cheap bodies, hold one real threat back, and keep a protection spell — you run five that are free or flash — for the turn you go all-in, not the turn after.

Combat is your second kill: the lords, Shared Animosity and Sanctum Seeker turn the same width into lethal attacks. The infinites are found money, not the plan — Bloodthirsty Conqueror with Vito or Sanguine Bond ends the game on the spot (stacks 004 and 006 prove it), but it assembles unassisted in 4.8% of games. Don't chase it. Tutors move the main kill from 41.7% to 57.7% by turn 6; spend them on the missing converter or doubler, and take the loop only when it's dealt to you.

combo_lines.002: The clause that decides this is CR 616.1: when two replacement effects both want the same token-creation event, the affected player — you — chooses which applies first, and CR 614.5 grants each exactly one application. The choice is therefore yours and immaterial: one token becomes two becomes four in either order. The record then closes two doors. The tokens are created, not cast, so eminence does not trigger again; and Vampire Socialite's entry clause reads each of them onto the battlefield with a counter. The holding, in plain English: one two-mana Vampire spell yields five bodies, and the loop the reader might fear — tokens re-triggering eminence — does not exist.
combo_lines.003: Two words decide this case: 'during your turn.' Bloodletter of Aclazotz's replacement applies to each opponent's life loss, once per loss event — and the trigger count is fixed at declaration under CR 508.3a: seven attacking Vampires is seven Sanctum Seeker triggers, each its own event, each doubled separately to 2 per opponent. Fourteen total. Your gain is not doubled; the text reaches only opponents' loss. Note what Edgar's counter trigger does not do: Sanctum Seeker drains a fixed 1, so the counters change the combat to come, never the drain. The holding: the 14-life opponent reaches exactly 0 on the seventh trigger and is removed by state-based actions — before a single blocker is declared.
combo_lines.004: The controlling fact is CR 603.3d: each new Vito trigger is a fresh instance, and a fresh instance chooses its own target. That is what lets the loop walk the table one opponent at a time. The record runs thirteen Vito resolutions: nine points end opponent 2 exactly, thirty end opponent 1 exactly, and the killing loss still triggers Bloodthirsty Conqueror — the chain crosses a death without breaking, and the win arrives via CR 104.2a. One honest cost is on the record: Conqueror is a creature, and every iteration passes priority, so instant-speed creature removal is a loop-breaker at any point. Where an opponent holds such an answer, the record is silent and so am I; here none was held, and the game ends with you at 60.
combo_lines.006: The third pairing, and the same handshake: Sanguine Bond plays Vito's part, gain converting to targeted loss under per-instance targeting (CR 603.3d). The arithmetic differs in one particular the record is careful about — three divides neither 11 nor 26, so each opponent dies with a single point of overkill, unlike stack 004's exact zeros. Thirteen Bond resolutions, the killing loss still triggering Conqueror, final life 58, win by CR 104.2a. The removal-window profile is the narrowest of the set: Bond is an enchantment, so exactly one half of this loop — Conqueror — is exposed to creature removal. The holding: the pairing is deterministic and lethal on the same terms as stack 004, with one fewer way to die.
combo_lines.007: The question of law: is the end step 'during your turn'? It is — the ending phase is the fifth phase of your turn (CR 500.1) — so Bloodletter doubles each opponent's loss from Throne of the God-Pharaoh's trigger. But the count comes first, and it is a tapped-creature count: Bloodletter itself did not attack, sits untapped, and contributes nothing. Seven tapped creatures, doubled independently per opponent to 14. The record then splits the table: the opponent at 9 leaves the game; the opponent at 15 survives at exactly 1, and CR 104.2a's condition — all opponents gone — is not met. The holding: partially refuted as a table-kill. This trigger ends players, not games, and the margin was one life.
combo_lines.008: This case turns on occurrence-counting under CR 603.2c: Purphoros triggers once for each creature that enters, not once per entry event. Four tokens entering the battlefield simultaneously is one event carrying four occurrences — four separate triggers — and the Vampire spell resolving afterward is a fifth. Five triggers at 2 is 10 damage to each opponent, all from a single {B}{B} cast through the verified 1-to-2-to-4 doubling of stack 002. Purphoros's own non-creature status is irrelevant to his trigger; a permanent's abilities function from the battlefield regardless. The holding: the 10-life opponent reaches 0 on the fifth resolution exactly, and had they died earlier, the remaining triggers would still have resolved against the survivor.
combo_lines.009: The same clause, asked to carry the whole game plan: an ability triggers once per occurrence (CR 603.2c), and this line contains three creature-entry events — two tokens entering as one event with two occurrences, then the spell itself. Three payoffs, nine triggered abilities. Per opponent: three Purphoros resolutions at 2, three Impact Tremors at 1, three Warleader's Call at 1 — twelve, exactly lethal to a pod at 12. Two silences in the record deserve notice: Cordial Vampire's own ability never fires, because nothing dies; and Warleader's Call's anthem adds nothing, because no combat occurs. The holding: the deck's primary plan — cheap Vampire into converters and a doubler — is a verified kill, not a metaphor, and it is exact.

card_roles.Edgar Markov: Your engine never leaves the command zone: every Vampire spell you cast mints a token, and stack 002 shows two doublers turning one mint into four bodies. Cast him late as a finisher — his attack trigger pumps the army you already built.
card_roles.Anointed Procession: Doubles every token event you own, eminence mints included. Land it before the big turn, not after — stack 009's exact-lethal line runs through it.
card_roles.Mondrak, Glory Dominus: Doubler number two, on a body that can buy indestructible. Stacked with Procession, one cast makes four tokens — the order is yours and the math is the same (stack 002).
card_roles.Elspeth, Storm Slayer: Doubler number three, plus her own Soldiers, a team-wide flying turn, and a -3 that answers a resolved threat. Protect her loyalty with your width.
card_roles.Ocelot Pride: One mana that turns any lifegain turn into an end-step token — and with the city's blessing it copies every token that entered this turn. Play it early; it gets silly late.
card_roles.Purphoros, God of the Forge: Two damage to each opponent per arriving body — stack 008 prices one two-mana Vampire at 10 per opponent through the doublers. He's usually not a creature, so sweepers miss him.
card_roles.Impact Tremors: Your cheapest converter. Turn-2 Tremors means every body for the rest of the game pings the whole table — untick nothing, just cast Vampires into it.
card_roles.Warleader's Call: Converter and anthem in one: the damage half kills without combat, the +1/+1 half makes the combat kill real. Stack 009 shows it composing with Tremors and Purphoros.
card_roles.Corpse Knight: Converter number four, as life loss rather than damage — and it hits each opponent. A Vampire body that makes every other body hurt.
card_roles.Witty Roastmaster: Converter number five. Redundancy IS the plan here: you see one of these effects by turn 6 in 62.6% of games because the deck runs five of them.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Every creature death — yours included — drains. He hits one player per death, so aim him; his real job is making the table's board wipe pay you.
card_roles.Cruel Celebrant: The wide death drain: each opponent loses 1 per death of yours. When a wipe is on the stack, count your creatures — that's damage the table eats for killing your board.
card_roles.Legion's Landing // Adanto, the First Fo: One mana for a lifelink body, then a land that mints one every turn. Transform it the turn you attack with three — it fixes white forever after.
card_roles.Mavren Fein, Dusk Apostle: Attack with one nontoken Vampire and he pays you a token — doubled by your multipliers. Free width every single combat.
card_roles.Bloodline Keeper // Lord of Lineage: A token engine every turn, and a +2/+2 lord once you have five Vampires. The flip costs {B} — plan a real black source, because Cavern of Souls' mana can't pay an activation.
card_roles.Charismatic Conqueror: Taxes everything your opponents deploy untapped: they tap it down or you get a lifelink Vampire. Either way you're not the one paying.
card_roles.Preacher of the Schism: Point him at the biggest life total and he mints a body; attack while you're ahead and he draws you cards. Attack whoever you'd attack anyway — he pays either way.
card_roles.Vampire Socialite: Somebody loses life almost every turn you take, so your Vampires enter with an extra counter — stack 002's tokens arrived as 2/2s. Menace makes her a fine early attacker too.
card_roles.Cordial Vampire: Every creature death, anywhere at the table, grows your whole tribe. Between your drains and Skullclamp, deaths are something you manufacture.
card_roles.Drana, Liberator of Malakir: First-strike flier who counters up every attacker before regular damage lands. Swing her early — the counters compound.
card_roles.Knight of the Ebon Legion: A one-drop that scales: someone loses 4 life most turns in this deck, and the pump ability makes him a real late threat on an empty draw.
card_roles.Vampire of the Dire Moon: Deathtouch plus lifelink for one mana — the best blocker rate in the 99, and every lifelink hit is trigger fuel for Vito.
card_roles.Indulgent Aristocrat: One-drop lifelinker carrying the deck's sac outlet: two mana turns a doomed token into a counter on every Vampire. Sacrifice in response to exile removal and get paid.
card_roles.Voldaren Epicure: One red mana: a body, a ping to each opponent, and a Blood token that loots away a flooded land later. Everything this deck wants, in miniature.
card_roles.Vampire Cutthroat: Skulk means he connects turn after turn, and every hit is lifegain — which Vito and Sanguine Bond turn into somebody else's problem.
card_roles.Champion of Dusk: Your biggest refill: draw a card per Vampire you control, life is the fee. Cast him after the swarm, not before — five bodies means five cards.
card_roles.Sanctum Seeker: Every attacking Vampire drains the whole table — stack 003 prices seven attackers at 14 life per opponent under Bloodletter. Protect him on the big swing; he's the combat kill's engine.
card_roles.Bloodletter of Aclazotz: Doubles opponents' life loss on your turn — combat, converters, drains, all of it (stacks 003 and 007). The triple-black cost is the hardest cast in the deck; sequence your black sources for him.
card_roles.Bloodthirsty Conqueror: The infinite's spine: with Vito or Sanguine Bond down, any lifegain ends the table (stacks 004 and 006). Alone he's still a 5/5 flying deathtouch that pays you for every point anyone loses.
card_roles.Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose: Every point you gain, a target opponent loses. Verified kill loop with Conqueror (stack 004); honest drain engine with any lifelinker; his activation can grant the team lifelink for the alpha strike.
card_roles.Sanguine Bond: Vito's text on an enchantment — harder to remove, same verified loop with Conqueror (stack 006). Redundancy for the found-money kill.
card_roles.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: End-step drain equal to your tapped creatures — a second combat's worth of loss after a wide attack, doubled under Bloodletter (stack 007). Only tapped bodies count, so attack first, then collect.
card_roles.Legion Lieutenant: A two-mana lord. Nothing clever — every token gets bigger, and you make a lot of tokens.
card_roles.Stromkirk Captain: Lord plus first strike for the whole tribe, which makes blocking your swarm a losing trade every time.
card_roles.Captivating Vampire: Lord with a theft engine: tap five untapped Vampires to steal the best creature on the table, permanently. Steal before you attack — the ability needs untapped bodies.
card_roles.Patchwork Banner: Anthem and fixer in one: +1/+1 for the tribe and a rock that makes any colour. Name Vampire and never look back.
card_roles.Shared Animosity: Attack with six Vampires and each gets +5/+0. This is the card that turns width into combat lethality in one turn — hold it for the turn it kills.
card_roles.Skullclamp: One mana turns any 1/1 token into two cards, and the death feeds Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant and Cordial Vampire on the way out. Clamp freely; you print bodies for a living.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Two cards for two mana and two life — life this deck banks back by the handful. Cast it whenever you're not spending the turn on board.
card_roles.Pact of the Serpent: Name Vampire, target yourself, and draw a card per Vampire you control. Time it like Champion of Dusk: after the swarm, and mind your life total under your own drains.
card_roles.Welcoming Vampire: A card per turn for doing what you already do — putting small creatures onto the battlefield. Eminence alone triggers her every turn you cast a Vampire.
card_roles.Caretaker's Talent: Draws off your token entries — again, eminence triggers it for free — and the levels copy your best token and anthem the rest. Level up only when the mana is idle.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Best card in the deck at finding the missing kill half. Default target: the converter or doubler you lack — tutors take the turn-6 kill from 41.7% to 57.7%, and the infinite pieces don't pay that well.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Same instruction as Demonic: fetch the missing converter or multiplier by default. It costs a turn of drawing the card, so fire it at an end step with a plan.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: A tutor whose fee is a creature — which in this deck triggers your death drains and costs a token, not a card. The cheapest Demonic you'll ever cast.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The wipe insurance. Hold it for the turn you've committed the board or the turn their sweeper is on the stack — phasing out costs them the whole spell.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free with your commander out: the board survives the wrath and the drains collected on nothing. Keep one white source untapped as a bluff even when you don't have it.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: With Edgar on the field you take both modes: a protection spell and a kill spell in one card. Lifelink plus double strike on a wide board is usually just lethal.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Indestructible for the team at instant speed — or four to the face when four is what's left. The cheapest way to make a sweeper cost them a card for nothing.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free with a commander you control: aim their removal at their own things, or retarget the drain aimed at your engine. Hold it; its whole value is that they can't see it.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Best single-target answer in the format. Spend it on the card that beats you — the stax piece or the blocker that walls your swarm — not the scariest thing on the table.
card_roles.Path to Exile: Swords number two. The land they get matters less than the trigger-doubler or combo piece you exiled.
card_roles.Despark: Answers most things worth answering at instant speed — anything four mana or more, exiled. Save it for the permanent your creatures can't attack through.
card_roles.Anguished Unmaking: Exiles any nonland permanent for three life — life you bank back. Your cleanest answer to an enchantment or artifact engine.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroy anything — including a land locking you out — and the 3/3 they get is a body your drains eventually tax. Breadth is the point: this answers what nothing else in the 99 can.
card_roles.Stroke of Midnight: Gift's twin for nonlands, and the 1/1 they keep is a joke against your board. Your fifth and sixth true answers are what let you spend the first four early.
card_roles.Winds of Abandon: The one-sided reset: overloaded, every creature you don't control leaves and you keep the swarm. The basics they fetch matter far less than the combat that follows.
card_roles.Olivia's Wrath: Your sweeper, and it's one-sided by trade — non-Vampires get -X/-X for your Vampire count. Know your own five non-Vampire bodies eat it too; the death drains collect on the way down.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless a turn from turn one. It casts the generic half of everything; it never pays a coloured pip, so don't count it toward Bloodletter.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any of your three colours, every turn, forever. The rock you always keep in an opener light on lands.
card_roles.Talisman of Indulgence: Black or red on demand for a point of life — and black is the colour you're short. Tap it for B and take the ping happily.
card_roles.Bontu's Monument: Discounts every black creature and drains the table on every creature cast — a sixth converter that only counts your casts, not your tokens. It makes each eminence turn cheaper AND heavier.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: Discounts every Vampire and digs one off the top each upkeep. In a deck where most cards share a type, it's ramp and card advantage at once.
card_roles.Command Tower: All three colours, no questions. The best land in the deck.
card_roles.Cavern of Souls: Any colour for creature spells, uncounterable — but that mana pays for SPELLS only. It cannot activate Castle Locthwain, flip Bloodline Keeper, or pay any ability. Name Vampire and know the limit.
card_roles.Mana Confluence: Any colour for one life. In a deck that drains life back constantly, pay it without blinking.
card_roles.City of Brass: Confluence's twin — a point of life per tap for perfect fixing. Same instruction: the drains repay it.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Whatever your other lands make. Nearly always all three colours by turn 3.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: Every land you have taps for black — the colour carrying half your pips. It quietly fixes Bloodletter's triple-B all by itself.
card_roles.Nomad Outpost: All three colours, enters tapped. Play it on a turn you weren't spending anyway.
card_roles.Savai Triome: Three colours and a fetchable type — grab it with a fetch land early, cycle it never.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Fetchable B/R dual. Pay the 2 life when you need it untapped; you'll get the life back.
card_roles.Godless Shrine: Fetchable W/B dual — the deck's two heaviest colours on one card.
card_roles.Sacred Foundry: Fetchable R/W dual. Third in the shock priority; fetch black first.
card_roles.Battlefield Forge: R or W untapped for a point of pain. Fine; the drains cover the tab.
card_roles.Caves of Koilos: W or B untapped for a point of pain — take it for black more often than not.
card_roles.Sulfurous Springs: B or R untapped for a point of pain. Same rule: black first.
card_roles.Silent Clearing: W/B pain land that becomes a card when the game goes long. Sacrifice it late before you flood.
card_roles.Blazemire Verge: B/R that's untapped whenever it matters in a deck this heavy on the pair.
card_roles.Bleachbone Verge: W/B, usually untapped, covering the two colours with the most pips.
card_roles.Concealed Courtyard: W/B untapped on the turns that decide aggro games — one through three.
card_roles.Haunted Ridge: B/R that's live from the mid-game on; sequence it after the slow lands.
card_roles.Shattered Sanctum: W/B, untapped with any other land in hand — which is nearly always.
card_roles.Sundown Pass: R/W with the same clause; play the basics and verges first.
card_roles.Luxury Suite: B/R, untapped in any multiplayer game — which is every game this deck plays.
card_roles.Spectator Seating: R/W with the same multiplayer clause. Untapped, effectively always.
card_roles.Vault of Champions: W/B with the same clause — a free Godless Shrine at a Commander table.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: A draw engine on a land — expensive per card, cheapest when your hand is empty, which is exactly when an aggro deck needs it. It needs REAL black mana, not Cavern's.
card_roles.Minas Tirith: Untapped behind any of your thirteen legends, and it draws a card whenever you attack with two — you attack with seven.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A black source that channels a dead late draw into your best fallen creature. The only graveyard text in the 99, and it points at your own yard.
card_roles.Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid: A black source or, late, a two-card refill priced at one token. Cast the sorcery when the board is wide and the land drop is spare.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana per turn for two life — turn-3 Edgar money. The drains buy the life back.
card_roles.Bloodstained Mire: Fetches the shock you're missing. Black first, as always.
card_roles.Marsh Flats: Fetches Godless Shrine or a basic — grab black-producing land unless white is the hole.
card_roles.Prismatic Vista: Fetches either basic, untapped, at the cost of one life. Take the Swamp four times out of five.
card_roles.Plains: One of two basics — the Winds of Abandon and fetch target for white.
card_roles.Swamp: Four copies feeding the colour with half the deck's pips. When a fetch asks, this is usually the answer.

mulligan:
You keep 80.8% of opening sevens, so mulligan decisions here are about spotting the bad fifth, not agonizing over every hand. The frame is simple: two to four lands, at least one black source, and something to cast on turns one and two. Eminence means your engine is already in hand every game — what you're looking for is fuel.

KEEP: two-plus lands with a one- or two-drop Vampire (Indulgent Aristocrat, Vampire Cutthroat, Voldaren Epicure, Knight of the Ebon Legion, Cordial Vampire, Vampire of the Dire Moon) and any converter or draw piece. A hand with Impact Tremors or Skullclamp and cheap bodies is a snap keep — that's the 62.6% turn-6 converter figure showing up early, and it's the whole game plan in seven cards.

SHIP: any hand with no black source. Black carries 39 of the deck's 76 coloured pips and the drain payoffs live there — a hand of Plains and red duals casts your worst cards and none of your best. Ship five-land hands too: your curve tops at six with a modal cost of three, and the deck refills through Skullclamp, Champion of Dusk and Pact of the Serpent, not through extra land drops.

The close calls: a slow hand with a doubler (Anointed Procession, Mondrak) and lands is keepable — the multiplier is the half of the kill you draw less urgently, and eminence provides the bodies. A hand of all payoffs and no cheap Vampires is the trap: converters convert entries, and with nothing to cast, nothing enters. When in doubt, keep the hand that casts a Vampire on turn one or two. The land drop holds at 91.9% through turn 3 — trust it.
upgrades:
Two numbers point at everything on this list: 27 and zero. Twenty-seven black sources against a Karsten target of 36 — 76.4% on-curve castability in the colour where every drain payoff lives — and zero answers to a graveyard, the one interaction class the 99 leaves open. Three of the ten move black mana; one, Soul-Guide Lantern, closes the graveyard for one colourless mana. Those four are plumbing, and plumbing is where a marginal dollar buys the most.

The rest are engine depth, and the headline is Exquisite Blood. The infinite currently rides on one body: Bloodthirsty Conqueror appears in 7.1% of opening sevens, and the line assembles unassisted in 4.8% of games. Add the enchantment and the pairings go from two to four — with Vito, Sanguine Bond and Conqueror all in the 99, every half suddenly has two partners — and both of its loops are checker-passed resolutions already on file. That's the cheapest consistency purchase available: not a new engine, a second copy of the one that's proven.

One famous card is absent on purpose. Rest in Peace would cover the graveyard gap for two mana, but under it creatures exile instead of dying — and a deck earning 62.6%-by-turn-6 conversion off entries and deaths cannot blank Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant and Cordial Vampire to answer somebody else's yard. The Lantern does the job without the friendly fire. The 99 is locked for a piloting-practice stretch, so read the ten below as a watch list priced in advance: each entry names what it closes, what it unlocks, and what it would naturally replace.
mana_base:
Thirty-seven land copies across 34 entries, and one ratio runs the show: black is 51.3% of the deck's pip demand on 42.9% of its sources. That's 27 black sources — 24 lands plus three rocks — against a Karsten double-pip target of 36, for 76.4% on-curve castability. Red is the mirror image, 14.5% of the pips on 25% of the sources. The white and red halves of this deck cast themselves; the black cards are the casts you plan, and the black cards are the drains.

The 90% yardstick deserves its footnote: it's priced against a 40-land deck casting on curve, so in a 37-land aggro list the 36-source figure isn't reachable — it's a direction, not a destination. The honest per-colour reading, rocks included: white 89.5%, red 83.1%, black 76.4%. That last number is what a triple-B Bloodletter and a double-black quorum cost in a three-colour deck that refuses to slow down for them.

Fifteen of 37 lands can enter tapped — 41%, over the one-in-three budget — but only three always do; the other twelve carry conditions this deck mostly meets (a multiplayer table, a second land in hand, a legend on board). The goldfish doesn't flinch: 91.9% hit the turn-3 land drop, mean available mana is 5.3 by turn 6, and the mulligan keeps 80.8% of sevens. Tapped-land pain here is a scheduling problem, not a screw problem — the cheap turns absorb it.

What the rocks actually buy: Sol Ring is generic-only and never pays a pip; Arcane Signet and Patchwork Banner cover all three colours; Talisman of Indulgence adds the black the deck is short, at a life per tap the drains repay. Herald's Horn and Bontu's Monument are discounts, not sources — the simulation doesn't model them, so every figure above is conservative by roughly their contribution.

Two fine-print items. Cavern of Souls makes coloured mana for creature SPELLS only — it cannot pay Castle Locthwain's draw, Bloodline Keeper's flip, or any activated cost, so it accelerates the tribe without powering the machinery. And City of Brass plus Mana Confluence charge a life per tap for perfect fixing — in a deck that banked 7 life across one verified attack (stack 003), that's the cheapest fixing money can buy.
threat_assessment:
They hear “Edgar Markov,” look at the empty seat where a six-mana commander should be, and they relax. Let them. They are pricing a deck that starts on turn six, and yours started on turn one.

Eminence works from the command zone: every Vampire spell you cast mints a body while Edgar sits at home. And he sits a long time — mean cast turn 6.6, on the battlefield by turn six in barely half your games — so stop building turns around him. Casting Edgar is a mid-game decision you make on your terms; the turn-six decision spread walks that exact call, and the answer is usually “not yet.”

The clock the table cannot see: two bodies by turn three, 4.2 by turn six, off cards that look like draft commons.

Here is the exact flip point. You stop being a creature deck the moment a creature entering costs all three seats life. Five cards do it — Purphoros, God of the Forge, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Corpse Knight, Witty Roastmaster. Land one while the table is watching someone else.

Stack 009 is why they are right to panic afterwards. Three converters, one Anointed Procession, one two-mana Vampire: nine triggers, twelve damage to every seat, no combat step anywhere in it. Read every cheap Vampire in your hand as a burn spell waiting on that layer.

So build the layer while it is cheap and boring. Impact Tremors on turn two reads as durdle and eats no removal. Corpse Knight looks like a bad two-drop right up until it is not. Slide Anointed Procession in behind them — it visibly does nothing the turn it resolves, which is exactly why it survives. Elspeth, Storm Slayer gets attacked on sight, so she comes down last and never first.

Pick your archenemy turn before you sit down. Converter plus multiplier is together by turn six in 41.7% of your games, 57.7% when a tutor buys the missing half — so aim the loud turn at four or five, spend Demonic Tutor or Vampiric Tutor on the missing half, and never aim it at whenever Edgar shows up.

Now the card that changes how you read held mana. Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant make every death a drain, your own deaths included. Know the split cold: Celebrant hits each opponent per death, Blood Artist drains one player of your choice — point him at whoever cast the wipe. With both down, a twelve-body board dying is twelve off every seat plus twelve more aimed wherever it hurts. The sweeper you are supposed to fear has your invoice stapled to it; the wipe-timing spread runs the arithmetic, and the answer is go.

So flip the standard read. A control seat holding five untapped lands after a quiet turn is holding a sweeper — believe it. But once a drain stands on your board, stop shrinking. Attack the sweeper holder, make the wrath a card they need instead of a card they choose, and rebuild from a zone no wipe touches.

Half your games you hold no protection by turn six — 50.0% on the record. In those games the drains ARE the protection, so deploy a drain before you deploy width. In the other half, know the discount: Flawless Maneuver and Deflecting Swat are free the moment Edgar is on the battlefield, so the turn you finally cast him is the turn you are safest, not just loudest.

What actually turns you off is not a wrath — it is the cheap permanent that taxes entries or stops life loss. Despark only reaches mana value four and up, so the cheap piece takes Generous Gift or Stroke of Midnight, spent on whatever is aimed at YOU. You hold one of those answers by turn six in only 42.8% of games; when one is in hand, it is not a spare.

Last, the mana that pays for all of it. Black is your thin colour — 27 sources against a 36-source yardstick, 76.4% on-curve for double black — and the drains and double-black lords are the black cards, so the shortage taxes your kill, never your filler. Take a Swamp-typed land off Bloodstained Mire, Marsh Flats and Prismatic Vista every time you are unsure, prize Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, and never plan Castle Locthwain's draw, Bloodline Keeper's flip or Captivating Vampire's activation onto Cavern of Souls — its coloured mana casts creature spells only.

Embrace the archenemy seat the day the machine is assembled, and it assembles in 57.4% of your games. On that day you are not the threat because the table says so. You are the threat because the arithmetic says so — and arithmetic wins these.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL: They believe the wrath answers you. Played right, it pays you. Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant see every death including their own, so a twelve-body board dying drains each opponent twelve through Celebrant and hands Blood Artist twelve triggers to aim at the caster — deploy a drain before you deploy width, then commit exactly what wins and welcome the wipe. Count the survivors too: Anointed Procession, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Caretaker's Talent, Patchwork Banner, Herald's Horn and Legion's Landing all stand through a creature wrath, Purphoros is indestructible, and eminence rebuilds a token per cast from the command zone. Hold Teferi's Protection for the wipe moment and nothing else; protection is in hand by turn six in only 50.0% of your games, so in the other half the drains are the policy — play like it. Two facts to know cold. Your own Olivia's Wrath kills Corpse Knight and Mondrak — five of your 29 creatures are not Vampires — so fire it at an opponent's board, never to tidy your own. And do not count Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubling the death drains under THEIR sweeper: his clause reads “during your turn,” and nothing on the record extends it to theirs.

VS STAX AND TAX: A tax hits the deck casting three spells a turn hardest, and that is you — 29 of your 63 spells cost two or less. Recount the hand under the tax before you sequence: a two-cast turn becoming one halves the eminence engine. You are the beatdown by force here — race the lock's completion, do not try to out-resource it. Lead Ancient Tomb, land Herald's Horn or Bontu's Monument for the rebate, and leave Edgar in the zone longest in this matchup: six-plus mana is the first thing a tax prices out, and the tokens have been arriving since turn one. Then name the piece that beats YOU — the one taxing creature entries or shutting off life loss — and spend the matching answer on it, not on the scariest thing showing: Despark cannot exile anything under mana value four, so the cheap piece takes Generous Gift or Stroke of Midnight, and Anguished Unmaking is reserved for the one you cannot afford to see resolve twice.

VS THE AGGRO MIRROR: Ask the two operational questions — who is faster, who has inevitability — and you usually keep the beatdown seat while gaining a defence they lack: your converters kill without a combat step, and every drain raises your total as it lowers theirs, pushing their damage-per-card below lethal. Let Vampire of the Dire Moon and Vampire Cutthroat hold the ground — deathtouch and lifelink make attacking you a losing trade — while Stromkirk Captain's first strike wins every even fight on your turn. Sanctum Seeker is the mirror-breaker: stack 003 prices a seven-Vampire attack at fourteen off each opponent at declare attackers, before a blocker matters. And assign roles per seat, not per game: beatdown against the ramp player, control against the faster aggro seat, in the same turn cycle.

VS COMBO: You hold no stack interaction, so the lever is the clock: the kill is assembled by turn six in 41.7% of games and 57.7% when a tutor buys the missing half — spend Demonic Tutor and Vampiric Tutor on the kill, never on your own loop. Your one trick is Deflecting Swat: it retargets a spell or ability, and it is free only while Edgar is on the battlefield — he lands on a mean turn 6.6, so budget three mana for it until then. Vampiric Tutor at the combo player's end step is your fastest response to a telegraphed win: one mana for the card that makes your next turn lethal. When you present, count the table's open mana and assume every held answer appears — then prefer the attack-plus-triggers kill that leaves a board behind over the Bloodthirsty Conqueror loop, which assembles on its own in 4.8% of games and rests on one 5/5 the table can kill at instant speed.

VS GRAVEYARDS, BOTH DIRECTIONS: Their hate is nearly dead against you — this 99 puts nothing in the yard on purpose, so a Bojuka Bog aimed your way exiles air; smile and say thank you. The one exception deserves respect: an exile-instead effect like Rest in Peace means your creatures never “die,” which mutes Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant — the entry converters and Sanctum Seeker's attack drain do not care, so shift the kill onto them and spend a noncreature answer on the exile piece only when the death drains are your live plan. Going the other way, you hold zero graveyard answers — confirmed down to the oracle text — so a reanimator seat is answered by clock, not cards: mark them the priority seat early, aim the converter damage there, and make their engine race yours.
